comp.label: The Swifts of Bellwether Lane
comp.compStory:
Every year, on or around the fifth of May, Mr Abara stood at the end of Bellwether Lane with a notebook and waited for the sky to change its mind.

Nadia had watched him do it since she was six. She had assumed, for most of those years, that he was simply a little odd. He was the sort of neighbour who wore a tie to put the bins out and who said "Good afternoon" as though he were reading it from a list of important announcements. But this spring she was eleven, and bored, and the end of the lane was as good a place as any to be bored in. So she went and stood beside him.

"What are we waiting for?" she asked.

"Swifts," said Mr Abara, without lowering his binoculars. "They've been in Africa all winter. They'll be here any day."

"How do you know they'll come back here? To this lane?"

"Because they always have." He paused. "Well. Fewer of them, every year. But always."

They waited for forty minutes and saw nothing but pigeons, which Mr Abara did not count. Nadia went home unimpressed.

The next evening, she went back.

On the third evening, just as the light was turning the colour of weak orange squash, there was a sound like someone tearing a sheet of paper very fast, high above the rooftops. Three dark shapes, shaped like anchors or like boomerangs, sliced across the sky and vanished behind the chimneys of number fourteen.

Mr Abara wrote something in his notebook. His hand, Nadia noticed, was not entirely steady.

"Is that it?" she said. "Three?"

"Three today," he said. "More tomorrow, if we're lucky." Then, more quietly: "Did you know that a young swift, once it leaves the nest, may not land again for two years? It eats in the air. It sleeps in the air. It only comes down when it is ready to build a nest of its own."

Nadia tried to imagine never touching the ground for two years. It made her feel slightly dizzy, as if the pavement had become less reliable.

"And they nest here?"

"Under the roof tiles of the old houses. There are gaps, you see, where the tiles meet the wall. Just big enough." He pointed with his pen at the long terrace opposite: number fourteen, number sixteen, number eighteen. "They have nested in those gaps for longer than anyone has lived in the houses."

It was a week later that the scaffolding went up around number sixteen.

Nadia saw the sign first: ROOF REPLACEMENT. Then she saw Mr Abara, standing very still on the pavement, reading it as though it were written in a language he had once known and since forgotten.

"New roof," he said, when she joined him. "New tiles. No gaps."

"Can't you tell them? The builders?"

"I'm a retired accountant, Nadia. I am not in the habit of telling people what to do with their roofs." He folded his notebook closed. "It is their house."

Nadia looked at the scaffolding, and at the dark gap under the old tiles, and at Mr Abara's tie, which was blue with small yellow birds on it. She had never noticed the birds before.

That night, she did something she had never done before: she read about swifts until her mother came in and turned off the light. She learned that they had lost more than half their numbers in Britain in the last few decades. She learned that this was partly because old buildings were being repaired, and new ones built without any gaps at all. And she learned that there were special bricks, hollow inside, which could be built into a wall to give a swift a place to nest.

The next morning she knocked on the door of number sixteen.

The woman who answered had paint on her hands and a baby on her hip. Nadia had prepared a speech. It began with "Excuse me" and contained the words "population decline" twice. By the end of it the woman was smiling, though Nadia could not tell whether that was a good sign or not.

"Swift bricks," the woman repeated. "I had no idea. Write it down for me, would you? I'll ask the builder."

Two weeks later, there was a new roof on number sixteen, as smooth and grey as a closed book. Mr Abara looked at it for a long time. Then Nadia took his arm, which she had never done before either, and walked him round to the side wall.

High up, just under the edge of the roof, there were three neat, dark slots in the brickwork.

Mr Abara said nothing at all. But that evening, at the end of Bellwether Lane, he handed Nadia the notebook and the pen.

"Your count," he said. "I'll hold the binoculars."

They counted eleven.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Around which date did Mr Abara wait for the swifts each year?
questions.optionA: The fifth of May
questions.optionD: The first of May
questions.optionE: The first of April
questions.explanation: The first line says 'on or around the fifth of May'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What did Nadia think of Mr Abara before this spring?
questions.optionA: She thought he was an expert on birds
questions.optionD: She thought he was a little odd
questions.optionE: She thought he was very funny
questions.explanation: 'She had assumed, for most of those years, that he was simply a little odd.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Mr Abara said "Good afternoon" "as though he were reading it from a list of important announcements". What does this suggest about him?
questions.optionA: He is rude to his neighbours
questions.optionB: He finds it hard to remember people's names
questions.optionD: He is shy and speaks very quietly
questions.optionE: He is very formal and serious in the way he speaks
questions.explanation: Reading 'important announcements' suggests a stiff, formal, serious manner, which fits his wearing a tie to put the bins out.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did Nadia first go and stand beside Mr Abara?
questions.optionA: She was bored and had nothing better to do
questions.optionC: Her mother told her to keep him company
questions.optionD: She wanted to learn about swifts
questions.optionE: She wanted to borrow his binoculars
questions.explanation: 'She was eleven, and bored, and the end of the lane was as good a place as any to be bored in.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did Mr Abara not count the pigeons?
questions.optionA: He was only recording swifts
questions.optionB: He could not see them clearly
questions.optionD: Nadia was counting them instead
questions.optionE: There were too many to count
questions.explanation: He was waiting for swifts, so the pigeons did not belong in his record.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The swifts made "a sound like someone tearing a sheet of paper very fast". What does this simile suggest?
questions.optionA: Their call was sharp, sudden and high-pitched
questions.optionB: They were carrying paper to their nests
questions.optionC: They were flying very low and slowly
questions.optionD: Their call was soft and gentle
questions.optionE: They were frightened of Mr Abara
questions.explanation: Tearing paper fast is a quick, harsh, ripping sound, like a swift's scream.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "His hand, Nadia noticed, was not entirely steady." Why might Mr Abara's hand have been shaking?
questions.optionA: He was moved and relieved that the swifts had returned
questions.optionB: He was nervous about talking to Nadia
questions.optionC: He was angry that only three had come
questions.optionD: He was tired from holding the binoculars
questions.optionE: He was cold because it was late in the evening
questions.explanation: After years of falling numbers, seeing the swifts return clearly affects him deeply.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: According to Mr Abara, how long might a young swift stay in the air without landing?
questions.optionA: Two weeks
questions.optionD: Forty minutes
questions.optionE: One whole winter
questions.explanation: 'A young swift, once it leaves the nest, may not land again for two years.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Nadia felt "as if the pavement had become less reliable". What does this show?
questions.optionA: The pavement on the lane was cracked and broken
questions.optionB: The idea of never landing was so strange that it unsettled her
questions.optionC: She did not believe what Mr Abara said
questions.optionD: She was about to fall over
questions.optionE: She wanted to fly like a swift
questions.explanation: Imagining life without touching the ground makes her feel dizzy, so even solid ground seems less certain.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Mr Abara read the sign "as though it were written in a language he had once known and since forgotten". What does this suggest?
questions.optionA: He was stunned and struggling to take in what it meant
questions.optionB: He was pleased about the new roof
questions.optionC: The sign was written in another language
questions.optionD: He could not read English very well
questions.optionE: He had forgotten his glasses
questions.explanation: He understands the words but is too shocked to accept what they mean for the swifts.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does Mr Abara refuse to speak to the builders?
questions.optionA: He has already spoken to them
questions.optionB: He is afraid of the builders
questions.optionC: He does not care about the swifts any more
questions.optionD: He feels it is not his place to tell people what to do with their own homes
questions.optionE: He thinks the swifts will find somewhere else
questions.explanation: 'I am not in the habit of telling people what to do with their roofs... It is their house.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Nadia notices that Mr Abara's tie has small yellow birds on it. Why is this detail important?
questions.optionA: It shows that he is wearing his best clothes
questions.optionB: It shows that Nadia wants a tie like it
questions.optionC: It shows how much birds really mean to him, which she had not realised before
questions.optionD: It explains why the builders ignored him
questions.optionE: It shows that he likes the colour yellow
questions.explanation: She 'had never noticed the birds before': she is beginning to see him, and his love of birds, properly.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Which of these is NOT given as a reason for the fall in swift numbers?
questions.optionA: People feeding them the wrong food
questions.optionC: Fewer places for them to nest
questions.optionD: New buildings being built without gaps
questions.optionE: Gaps under roof tiles being closed
questions.explanation: The passage blames repairs and new buildings that leave no gaps; feeding is never mentioned.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Nadia's speech included the words "population decline". What do these words mean?
questions.optionA: A change in what animals eat
questions.optionB: A fall in the number of animals
questions.optionC: A group of people who live together
questions.optionD: A rise in the number of animals
questions.optionE: The movement of animals to another country
questions.explanation: A population is how many there are; a decline is a fall.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why could Nadia not tell whether the woman's smile was "a good sign or not"?
questions.optionA: The woman had paint on her face
questions.optionB: The woman might have been smiling because she was amused rather than convinced
questions.optionC: The woman did not speak English
questions.optionD: The woman was smiling at her baby
questions.optionE: Nadia could not see the woman clearly
questions.explanation: A child giving a serious, rehearsed speech could make an adult smile kindly, so Nadia cannot be sure she has been taken seriously.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The new roof was "as smooth and grey as a closed book". What does this suggest at first?
questions.optionA: That there seemed to be no openings left for the swifts
questions.optionB: That the roof was easy to climb
questions.optionC: That the roof was badly built
questions.optionD: That the house was a library
questions.optionE: That the builders had painted it
questions.explanation: A closed book has no gaps; the reader fears the swifts have been shut out, until the bricks are revealed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How has Nadia changed by the end of the story?
questions.optionA: She has gone from being bored by the swifts to taking action to protect them
questions.optionB: She has stopped caring about the swifts
questions.optionC: She has decided to become an accountant
questions.optionD: She has fallen out with Mr Abara
questions.optionE: She has become afraid of birds
questions.explanation: She begins 'unimpressed' but researches swifts, speaks to the neighbour and helps secure the swift bricks.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does Mr Abara hand Nadia the notebook and pen at the end?
questions.optionA: Because he wanted to stop counting swifts
questions.optionC: To show that he trusts her to carry on the work he cares about
questions.optionD: Because Nadia asked to borrow them
questions.optionE: Because he could no longer see the birds
questions.explanation: Handing over 'your count' passes on his yearly tradition to her.

questions.quest: What is 1,428 ÷ 7?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 5/6 − 3/8?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 3/5 of 85?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A coat costs £80. In a sale the price is reduced by 15%. What is the sale price?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: 42 sweets are shared between Kit and Sam in the ratio 3 : 4. How many does Sam get?
questions.explanation: There are 7 parts, so one part is 6. Sam gets 4 × 6 = 24.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: If a = 6 and b = 7, what is 3a − 4(a − b)?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the 8th term of the sequence 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, …?
questions.explanation: Each term is one more than a square number (1+1, 4+1, 9+1, …). The 8th is 8² + 1 = 65.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the mean of 12, 15, 9, 15, 11, 16 and 13?
questions.explanation: The total is 91 and there are 7 numbers: 91 ÷ 7 = 13.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles of 38°. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°: 180 − 38 − 38 = 104°.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: This shape is made of rectangles. What is its area? (All corners are right angles.)

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the perimeter of the same shape?
questions.stemFigure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 250 185" width="300" height="222"><polygon points="40,20 130,20 130,90 210,90 210,150 40,150" fill="#e0f2fe" stroke="#1f2937" stroke-width="2"/><text x="85" y="14" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1f2937">9 cm</text><text x="125" y="166" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1f2937">17 cm</text><text x="20" y="88" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#1f2937">13 cm</text><text x="216" y="124" font-size="11" fill="#1f2937">6 cm</text><text x="125" y="180" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6b7280">Not drawn to scale</text></svg>

questions.optionD: 45 cm

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A jug holds 2.5 litres of juice. Three glasses of 650 ml are poured out. How much juice is left?
questions.optionD: 450 ml
questions.optionE: 550 ml

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A train leaves at 07:52 and the journey takes 95 minutes. When does it arrive?
questions.explanation: 95 minutes = 1 hour 35 minutes. 07:52 + 1 h = 08:52; + 35 min = 09:27.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: How many prime numbers are there between 30 and 50?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: One bell rings every 4 minutes and another rings every 6 minutes. They both ring at 10:00. When will they next ring together?
questions.explanation: The lowest common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12, so they next ring together 12 minutes later.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: The point (3, −2) is reflected in the x-axis. Where does it end up?
questions.explanation: Reflecting in the x-axis keeps the x-coordinate and changes the sign of the y-coordinate.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A bag holds 4 red, 7 blue and 9 green counters. One is taken at random. What is the probability that it is blue?
questions.explanation: There are 20 counters and 7 are blue, so the probability is 7/20.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: I think of a number, multiply it by 4 and subtract 7. The answer is 45. What was my number?
questions.explanation: Work backwards: 45 + 7 = 52, then 52 ÷ 4 = 13.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Ruby buys 6 notebooks at £3.45 each and 2 pens at £1.80 each. She pays with a £50 note. How much change does she get?

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, CAT is written as DCW. How would LAMP be written in the same code?
questions.optionA: MCPT
questions.optionD: NCPT
questions.optionE: MCPS
questions.explanation: The 1st letter moves on 1, the 2nd moves on 2, the 3rd moves on 3, and so on: L→M, A→C, M→P, P→T.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, FROG is written as HTQI. Using the same code, what does UYCP stand for?
questions.optionA: SPAN
questions.optionD: SWAN
questions.optionE: SCAN
questions.explanation: Each letter moves on 2 to make the code, so move each code letter back 2: U→S, Y→W, C→A, P→N.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next pair of letters: AZ, CX, FU, JQ, ?
questions.optionA: OM
questions.optionD: NL
questions.optionE: OK
questions.explanation: The first letters go forward 2, 3, 4, 5 (A, C, F, J, O). The second letters go back 2, 3, 4, 5 (Z, X, U, Q, L).

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, ?
questions.explanation: Two series take turns, and each doubles: 3, 6, 12, 24 and 4, 8, 16, 32.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 2, 5, 11, 23, 47, ?
questions.explanation: Each number is doubled and then 1 is added: 47 × 2 + 1 = 95.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
The numbers in each group are related in the same way. Find the missing number.
8 (19) 3     7 (17) 3     9 ( ? ) 4
questions.explanation: Double the first number and add the second: 8 × 2 + 3 = 19, 7 × 2 + 3 = 17, 9 × 2 + 4 = 22.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Three letters that make a word have been taken out of the word in capitals. Which three letters complete it?
In winter she wore a thick, woolly SF around her neck.
questions.optionA: PIT
questions.optionD: ORE
questions.optionE: ARK
questions.explanation: S + CAR + F = SCARF.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Find the word that completes the third pair in the same way as the first two.
(pain, pin)   (fear, far)   (beat, ?)
questions.optionA: bet
questions.optionD: eat
questions.optionE: bit
questions.explanation: The second letter is removed each time: pain → pin, fear → far, beat → bat.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Choose one word from each group that are closest in meaning.
(brave, happy, tired)   (weary, angry, cowardly)
questions.optionA: brave, weary
questions.optionD: brave, cowardly
questions.optionE: tired, weary
questions.explanation: Tired and weary both mean in need of rest. Brave and cowardly are opposites.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Choose one word from each group that are most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning.
(scarce, noisy, heavy)   (loud, plentiful, weighty)
questions.optionA: scarce, plentiful
questions.optionD: noisy, weighty
questions.optionE: heavy, weighty
questions.explanation: Scarce means in short supply; plentiful means there is a lot. Noisy/loud and heavy/weighty mean the same.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Three of these words go together. Which TWO do not belong?
cod   salmon   whale   trout   dolphin
questions.optionA: whale, dolphin
questions.optionD: salmon, whale
questions.optionE: trout, dolphin
questions.explanation: Cod, salmon and trout are fish. Whales and dolphins are mammals.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
A five-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which pair hides it?
"Do you like this tone of voice?"
questions.optionA: this tone
questions.optionD: like this
questions.optionE: tone of
questions.explanation: thi(S TONE) hides STONE.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: AC is to FH as LN is to ?
questions.optionA: QR
questions.optionD: QS
questions.optionE: RS
questions.explanation: Each letter moves forward 5 places: A→F, C→H, so L→Q and N→S.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: If the day after tomorrow is Saturday, what day was it the day before yesterday?
questions.optionA: Thursday
questions.optionD: Monday
questions.optionE: Tuesday
questions.explanation: Today is Thursday (two days before Saturday), so the day before yesterday was Tuesday.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Five children ran a race. Ella finished last. Ben finished after Dev but before Cara. Ali finished immediately before Cara. Who came third?
questions.optionA: Ella
questions.optionD: Ali
questions.optionE: Ben
questions.explanation: The only order that fits is Dev, Ben, Ali, Cara, Ella, so Ali came third.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: If A = 3, B = 5, C = 10, D = 15 and E = 25, what is (A × B) + C? Give your answer as a letter.
questions.optionA: A
questions.optionD: D
questions.optionE: E

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Here are three words and the codes for two of them, in no particular order.
TEAM   MEAT   MATE        2716   6127
What is the code for TAME?
questions.explanation: MEAT and TEAM both have E then A in the middle, but the two codes do not share middle digits, so the codes must belong to one of them and MATE. Only TEAM = 2716 and MATE = 6127 agree: T = 2, E = 7, A = 1, M = 6. So TAME = 2167.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Two words must swap places for the sentence to make sense. Which two?
The oven took the cake out of the baker.
questions.optionA: oven, baker
questions.optionD: took, baker
questions.optionE: cake, oven
questions.explanation: The baker took the cake out of the oven.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Which word goes equally well with both pairs of words?
(look, observe)   (clock, timer)
questions.optionA: alarm
questions.optionD: hour
questions.optionE: watch
questions.explanation: You watch (look at) something, and a watch tells the time.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next pair of letters: CE, FI, IM, LQ, ?
questions.optionA: OV
questions.optionD: OT
questions.optionE: OU
questions.explanation: The first letters go forward 3 each time (C, F, I, L, O); the second go forward 4 (E, I, M, Q, U).
